Judicial Branch Testimony Against LD 739, An Act to Reimburse the City of
Ellsworth for an Access Road to a New Court Facility in Hancock County
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Judiciary, my name is Barbara Cardone, and I am the Director of Legal Affairs and
Public Relations for the Maine Judicial Branch. I would like to provide the following
testimony against this bill.
This bill is erroneous drafted in putting the expense for the reimbursement under the
Judicial Branch budget. The bill is intended to ask the State to reimburse the City of Ellsworth for the cost of building a public road that will lead to areas of future
development. One building to be developed on that roadway may be a new
courthouse, if the City and the Judicial Branch reach agreement on other issues. This
is NOT a private roadway leading to a courthouse.
To be clear, the Judicial Branch has no objection to the State reimbursing the City, but
the reimbursement should be categorized under a different department in the budget (perhaps the Department of Transportation?) and not under the Judicial Branch.
Given the circumstances behind this bill, the Judiciary Committee may wish to
reference it to a committee with jurisdiction over public roads, or perhaps to a
committee that deals with issues between state and local government. The Judicial Branch also respectfully requests that the cost for the reimbursement be reassigned to
the appropriate department's budget.
Thank you for your consideration.

THE MAINE SENATE
132nd Legislature
Testimony of Senator Nicole Grohoski
In Support of LD 739, "An Act to Reimburse the City of Ellsworth
for an Access Road to a New Court Facility in Hancock County"
Before the Committee on Judiciary 10 March 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Judiciary, my name is Nicole Grohoski, and I proudly represent Senate District 7, which
includes 22 coastal communities in Downeast Maine, 21 of which are in Hancock County. Today,
I am pleased to testify as a cosponsor in support of LD Z32, "An Act to Reimburse the City of Ellsworth for an Access Road to a New Court Facility in Hancock County."
As our colleague Rep. White testified, Hancock County is in dire need of a new courthouse. Thank you to members of this committee and the full 131st Legislature who approved funding for a new courthouse for our county as well as consolidated courthouses in Androscoggin and
Somerset Counties.
Today I am back with another funding request, albeit a much smaller one. This bill would
reimburse the City of Ellsworth for the construction of a public road to access a property that our
City Council and many residents prefer for the new courthouse. Specifically, the bill would authorize reimbursement of 50% of the costs incurred to build the road, not to exceed $750,000. To be clear, the road would be a public road in the City of Ellsworth, not a road owned by the Judicial Branch, which is why they cannot bond for it.
Since we last met on the topic of a new Hancock County courthouse, a lot has transpired. After
an extensive, multi-year search, the Judicial Branch purchased a piece of property that was a bit
outside of our downtown and major commercial areas. Many folks who lived in that area
objected, mainly due to traffic and other public safety concerns. The City and Judicial Branch began Working together to see if any other options existed that might be more preferable for Ellsworth residents. The City identified a property with a willing seller off of High Street (US
Route 1) and is now facilitating a land swap agreement with the Judicial Branch.

However, to develop this property, a road will need to be built across other properties. On
January 7th, the Ellsworth City Council voted to move forward with funding for the road and continuing land swap negotiations. Rep. White and I agreed to pursue a state funding match to
offset the full burden to Ellsworth property taxpayers of a road built primarily to serve residents
of all of Hancock County (pop. ~5 6,000, compared to Ellsworth at ~9,000), which is why we are
here today.
It has come to our attention that the Judicial Branch has concerns about how the bill was drafted
and does not believe the reimbursement should be within their purview because this is a public
road, not an access road that would be owned by the Judicial Branch. Perhaps the Department of Transportation or the Department of Administrative and Financial Services would be better
suited to administer such a reimbursement. In light of this information, we could propose an
amendment to clarify that the road would be a City road and another agency (to be confirmed) would administer the reimbursement.
Fundamentally, it is fair for the state to participate in a cost-share with the City of Ellsworth to build a road to a state-owned asset that serves the whole of Hancock County. I ask for your support of this bill and commit to working with Rep. White to address the drafting concems raised by the Judicial Branch.
Thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony. I would be happy to answer any
questions.

Testimony on L.D. 739, "An Act to Reimburse the City of Ellsworth for an Access Road to a
New Court Facility in Hancock County"
Presented by Representative Russell P. White
District 13
Iudiciary Committee Monday, March 10, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and distinguished members of
the Ioint Standing Committee on Iudiciary:

I am State Representative Russell P. White, and I proudly represent District 13,
Central Hancock, Ellsworth, and Waltham. It is an honor to appear before you today
for the purpose of introducing L.D. 739, "An Act to Reimburse the City of Ellsworth for an Access Road to a New Court Facility in Hancock County."
Last year, Senator Grohoski was able to secure funding for a new courthouse facility
for Hancock County -- a much-needed investment. The existing courthouse was built in
1931, and although it is truly a beautiful work of architecture, it now boasts numerous
safety, space, electrical, parking, and mechanical deficiencies that negatively impacts court operations and public service. So, its replacement is a good thing; however, it also began a debate over where the courthouse should be located.

Land was purchased on the Surry Road, in a primarily residential area, and that

sparked a resistance from the nearby residents. There were several public hearings,

including many meetings with local and State personnel about relocating the

courthouse to a more amenable location.

,

Now, to my knowledge, it has been announced that the preferred location, for the
city anyway, is off High Street, in Ellsworth -- a business area, more accessible, with better traffic flow, etc.. The location is "off" High Street and would require an access road. Estimates have put the road at $1.2 to $1.4 million.
There are a couple of reasons why we are asking for assistance.
First, the original location for the new courthouse that the State chose was in a
residential area with massive resistance from the locals, and the lot was purchased prior to the knowledge of the neighborhood, thus sparking protest from the neighborhood and a high number of Ellsworth citizens. As such, a land swap had to be accommodated to make this a possibility, and the City of Ellsworth will be absorbing a high cost to make that happen. I humbly ask the State for 50% of the cost of the needed access road, up to an amount of $750,000.
The second reason is the overall cost of the land swap and access road would adversely affect the citizens of Ellsworth that already have a fairly high tax burden.
It is my understanding that this panel may potentially redirect this bill to the
Transportation Committee. I totally understand that vein of thinking and ask if this becomes a reality, that you would please do so with a recommendation of approval.
Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.
